name: Parmenion
bio: Parmenion is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century AD. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of the Wreath of Philippus, the Garland compiled in the first century AD.
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 183, 184, 239).

poems.title: Book VII, 183
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: (As she had just loosed her maiden zone) Death came first and took the maidenhood of Crocale. The bridal song ended in wailing, and the fond anxiety of her parents was set to rest not by marriage but by the tomb.

poems.title: Book VII, 184
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: I am the tomb of the maiden Helen, and in mourning too for her brother who died before her I receive double tears from their mother. To her suitors I left a common grief; for the hope of all mourned equally for her who was yet no one’s.

poems.title: Book VII, 239
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: It is a lying report that Alexander is dead if Phoebus be true. Not even Hades can lay hand on the invincible.

poems.title: Book IX, 43
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: The simple covering of my cloak is enough for me; and I, who feed on the flowers of the Muses, shall never be the slave of the table. I hate witless wealth, the nurse of flatterers, and I will not stand in attendance on one who looks down on me. I know the freedom of scanty fare.

poems.title: Book IX, 69
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: A stepmother’s spite is ever mordant, and not gentle even in love. I know what befel chaste Hippolytus.

poems.title: Book IX, 113
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: The bugs fed on me with gusto till they were disgusted, but I myself laboured till I was disgusted, dislodging the bugs.

poems.title: Book IX, 114
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: A child was peeping down from the very edge of a high tiled roof (Death has no fears for little children), when its mother from behind turned away its attention by showing it her breast. Thus one fount of milk twice beoowed life on her child.

poems.title: Book IX, 304: On the Battle of Thermopylae
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: Him who, transforming the paths of land and ocean, sailed over the dry land and marched on the sea, three hundred valiant Spartan spears resisted. Shame on you, mountains and seas bo

poems.title: Book IX, 342
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: An epigram of many lines does not, I say, conform to the Muses’ law. Seek not the long course in the short stadion. The long race has many rounds, but in the stadion sharp and short is the strain on the wind.

poems.title: Book XI, 4
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: A certain man, having married a woman who is complaisant to his neighbour only, snores and feeds. That was the way to get a living easily—not to go to sea, not to dig, but to snore off one’s dinner with a comfortable stomach, fattened richly at the expense of another.

poems.title: Book XI, 65
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: It is difficult to choose between famine and an old woman. ‘To hunger is terrible, but her bed is still more painful. Phillis when starving prayed to have an elderly wife, but when he slept with her he prayed for famine. Lo the inconstancy of a portionless son !

poems.title: Book XIII, 18
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.note: Paton’s metre label: ‘Hexameters followed by hendecasyllables’.
poems.text: Thou work of brass, be known as the prize of the swift filly, who when, torn by the spur, she had thrown her jockey, ran unmounted round the level course. And therefore did Parmenon gain golden victory. Phocritus, to thy son did the Lords of Amyclae grant to win in the race like his father.

poems.title: Book XVI, 216: On a Statue of Hera
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: Polycleitus of Argos, who alone saw Hera with his eyes, and moulded what he saw of her, revealed her beauty to mortals as far as was lawful; but we, the unknown forms beneath her dress’s folds, are reserved for Zeus.

poems.title: Book XVI, 222: On the Same
poems.author: Parmenion
poems.text: I, the stone of whom the Medes hoped to make a trophy, was changed opportunely to the form of Nemesis, the goddess justly planted on the shore of Rhamnus to be a witness to the Attic land of victory and the skill of her artist.
